A news article reports the collapse of a Hawaii investment firm, Bishop, Baldwin, Rewald, Dillingham and Wong. Hundreds of investors lost their life savings in the firm. After the collapse, CIA lawyers moved to seal the firm's records. The agency's connection to the company became the story's center. The publication is not identified.

The Rewald case joined finance and intelligence in one scandal. A firm that sold investments also, its founder claimed, served the CIA. Sealed records kept the public from testing that claim in full. The article preserves the collapse as first reported: the losses, the lawyers, and the seal. It is a period account of a case where the paper trail itself was treated as a secret.
podcast-joerogan-XJGKdkQ25CI:
Thousands of JFK files released by the National Archives get covered in a segment of the Joe Rogan Experience. The document dump was required by law and long delayed. When it landed, researchers and the curious dove in at once, and Rogan followed the story.

The talk sorts what the release held: fresh pages, old pages with fewer black bars, and the files still held back. Rogan asks why a democracy needs sixty years to open its own records. The segment is a dated dispatch from a disclosure day, useful for anyone tracking how the Kennedy paper trail has grown.
podcast-joerogan-lAYYmfoyLCI:
Aubrey Marcus sits with Rogan for episode 621 of the Joe Rogan Experience, an early talk on mind, body, and the examined life. Marcus had built Onnit, a fitness firm with a philosophy arm, and he was becoming a voice for optimization long before the word was everywhere.

The two talk training, purpose, and the habits Marcus credits for his drive, in the loose style of the young show. Rogan knows him as a friend and fellow seeker, and it shows. The episode is a fossil of the pre-optimization era, kept for listeners curious about where Marcus's later empire of self-work began.
